title: How to Minister to the Dying
subtitle: On bedside ministry, the last days of a believer, and how a pastor accompanies a person to the edge of death with honesty and hope

sections.title: The Room You Cannot Avoid
sections.body:
Sooner than you expect, the phone will ring and a voice will say it is time to come. Not for a meeting. For a death. The breathing has changed and the family has gathered and someone remembered that there is a pastor, and the pastor is you.

You will not feel ready. You will never feel ready. Go anyway.

Ministry to the dying is the work that no conference prepares you for and no book finishes teaching you. It is the most human room you will ever enter and the most holy. I have walked into it shaking. I have stood in the hallway outside the door and prayed for the courage to turn the handle, because I knew that on the other side was a person leaving and a family breaking and nothing I could say that would make either thing untrue. That fear is not a flaw. That fear is the right weight of the moment. The pastor who strides into a deathbed unafraid has forgotten where he is. You are standing at the border of two worlds, and the only thing you bring is the One who has crossed it already and come back.

sections.title: Tell the Truth, and Tell It Gently
sections.body:
The dying often know before anyone admits it. They feel the body letting go. What they need from you is not a brochure of false cheer. They need a person who will not lie to them.

Do not say you will be fine. You do not know that, and they can tell you are scared to say the true thing.

There is a kind of pastoral kindness that is really cowardice wearing a soft voice. It cannot bear the grief in the room, so it papers over death with empty reassurance, and the dying person is left more alone than before, because now they cannot even speak the truth they already know. Be the one who can say the word. You are very sick. You may be dying. And I am not going anywhere. The Bible does not flinch from death. It calls it the last enemy. It does not pretend the enemy is a friend. But it also says the enemy is defeated, and a defeated enemy can still be named out loud. I have learned to ask the dying a question most people are afraid to ask. Are you afraid. And then to sit in whatever answer comes.

sections.title: Bring the Old Words, Not New Ones
sections.body:
This is not the hour for your cleverness. The dying do not need an original thought. They need the words the church has spoken over the dying for two thousand years, because those words were carved deep enough to hold.

Read Scripture slowly. Pray the prayers their childhood remembers. Say nothing that needs explaining.

The twenty-third Psalm was made for this room. The valley of the shadow of death is not a metaphor here. It is the bed. Read it slowly, even if they seem past hearing, because hearing is the last sense to leave and the cadence of those words may have been planted in them before they could read. Read the fourteenth chapter of John, where Jesus says he goes to prepare a place. Read the great promise of Romans eight, that nothing can separate them from the love of God in Christ, not death, not life, not anything in all creation. These words are not information. They are a hand to hold in the dark. I have watched a face that had not responded in hours soften at the sound of words it learned as a child. The old words go deeper than the coma. They reach the place that is still listening.

sections.title: Care for the Ones Keeping Watch
sections.body:
There is more than one sufferer in the room. The family is dying too, in their own way, and they will carry this scene for the rest of their lives. How you serve them in these hours will be remembered when every sermon is forgotten.

Give them permission. Tell them it is good to speak to the dying. Tell them it is good to say goodbye.

Families freeze at the deathbed because no one has told them what to do. Help them. Encourage them to say the four things that need saying. I love you. Thank you. I forgive you. Goodbye. Sometimes a dying person holds on because they sense the family cannot release them, and a word of permission from a son or a wife frees them to go. Be the one who quietly makes that possible. And when the breathing stops, do not rush. Let the room be silent. Resist the urge to fill the holy quiet with management. There will be time for the practical. First there must be time for the weight. I have stood in that silence feeling that I had done nothing. I had done the only thing. I had stayed.

sections.title: The Hope That Survives the Grave
sections.body:
You can walk into that room because of an empty tomb. Take away the resurrection and the deathbed is a place of pure horror, and the pastor is a liar in a clerical collar. But the tomb is empty, and that one fact is why you can sit at a dying bed and not despair.

You are not pretending death is small. You are announcing that death is not final.

Jesus stood at the grave of his friend and wept, and then he called the dead man out by name. He did both. He grieved death as the obscenity it is and he overturned it as the conquered enemy it became. That is the ground you stand on at every bedside. You weep, because death is real and the loss is real and the love that is being torn is real. And you hope, because the one you serve has been through that door and holds the keys to it now. So go to the dying. Hold their hand. Tell them the truth and tell them the hope. Walk them as far as you can walk, to the edge of the country you cannot yet enter, and then hand them to the Shepherd who is already standing on the other side.
